facts: The paper is authored by researchers from the University of Stavanger and Amazon.
Weronika Łajewska is the lead author of the paper.
The research addresses the challenge of compressing prompts for Large Language Models.
The work aims to maintain critical information integrity during prompt compression.
The paper addresses prompt compression in large language models.
The authors developed an evaluation framework assessing compression methods across three dimensions.
They achieved gains of up to +23% in downstream performance with their improved soft prompting method.
The findings indicate that soft prompting with sequence-level training offers the best balance between compression effectiveness and rate.
Recent advances in large language models enable their application to tasks requiring long-context inputs.
The paper proposes a holistic evaluation framework assessing prompt compression across three dimensions.
Modifications to xRAG achieve a 23% improvement on downstream tasks.
PISCO offers the best compression-effectiveness trade-off among the methods evaluated.
Prompt compression techniques improve LLM efficiency by creating reduced-size prompt representations.
Hard prompting methods include demonstration selection, token refinement, and syntax-guided compression.
Soft prompting techniques achieve higher compression rates but lack interpretability.
This work advances evaluation methodology by measuring response grounding in original inputs.
The evaluation framework introduces more challenging tasks including long-form QA, document summarization, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
The framework measures compression quality using metrics like BERTScore and Exact Match.
FABLES is used to assess the faithfulness of claims to source material in the evaluation framework.
Table 2 presents performance results comparing various compression methods across multiple datasets including HotpotQA and arXiv summarization.
The study analyzes four prompt compression methods: xRAG, PISCO, and LLMLingua.
All compression methods cause significant performance losses ranging from 3-55%.
Compression methods result in 30-50 point drops in groundedness scores.
xRAG has a BERTScore F1 of 0.66 for reconstructing original contexts.
The xRAG prompt compression method struggled to preserve detailed information in long-context scenarios.
Sentence-level Pre-Training and Fine-Tuning yielded 1-5 point improvements across downstream tasks.
The Two-Step Pre-Training method achieved a 23% relative improvement on HotpotQA.
The baseline method reconstructed 13% of entities compared to 50% with the Two-Step Pre-Training.
Current compression methods, particularly xRAG, fail to preserve detailed information in long-context scenarios.
The authors suggest using sequence-level distillation to better integrate information across separate units.
One proposed direction is to dynamically adjust compression rates based on input complexity.
The authors recommend combining hard compression with soft prompting to reduce information loss.
The paper evaluates prompt compression methods in long-context generation tasks.
LLMLingua is a state-of-the-art hard compression approach discussed in the paper.
The proposed improvements to the xRAG method achieved up to a 23% improvement on downstream tasks.
The improvements resulted in a 2.7x better entity preservation compared to previous methods.
Experiments in the study are restricted to the Mistral-7B model.
The analysis focuses exclusively on English benchmarks.
Only one representative baseline per compression technique category is evaluated.
Long-form question-answering scenarios require further exploration.
The study used the Mistral-7B Instruct v0.2 model for prompt compression in LLMs.
The research trained models on two instances with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs each for approximately 16 hours per run.
Evaluation was conducted across five datasets: HotpotQA, arXiv-summarization, QuAC, TriviaQA, and GSM8K.
The Two-Step PT + FT variant of xRAG significantly improves ROUGE scores on out-of-domain examples.
